items.prompt: In the poster story, who held the power over which idea the class used?
choices: Theo, because he was loudest
The teacher, who could approve it
Priya, because her idea was objectively the best
items.explanation: The teacher was the only one who could say yes. Theo borrowed her attention and Priya never reached it.

items.prompt: What does this unit mean by power?
choices: Being the most liked person in the whole group
Holding the highest official title in the room
The ability to get something adopted and funded
items.explanation: Power is about making things happen, such as getting resources assigned or a proposal prioritized.

items.prompt: Is power the same thing as rank?
choices: No, rank is one source but not the definition
Yes, whoever has the higher rank always wins
Yes, though only inside very large companies
items.explanation: A title can provide power, but power is the ability to act, and people without titles can hold some of it.

items.prompt: Why did Priya's idea not get credited to her?
choices: The idea was technically wrong in a hidden way
It never reached the decider in a way that counted
The teacher disliked the topic of the poster
items.explanation: Nothing was wrong with the idea. The failure was in how it reached the person who decides.

items.prompt: The teacher holds power over the poster. Who holds it over the lunch menu?
choices: The teacher, as power follows people
Theo, because he already got credit once before
Someone else, whoever decides the menu
items.explanation: Power is situational. It belongs to whoever can act on that particular decision.

items.prompt: A correct idea reaches nobody who can act on it. What happens?
choices: It is shelved: right, but unadopted
It is funded at a later date
It gets adopted as soon as it is old enough
items.explanation: Correctness gets an idea to the gate and does not carry it through.

items.prompt: Which of these is a resource that power lets someone allocate?
choices: Being right about the facts
Budget, people and priorities
A loud voice in meetings
items.explanation: Power is the capacity to assign real resources, not just to hold opinions.

items.prompt: Does holding power make someone a bad person?
choices: Yes, it always corrupts
Yes, but only when they hold an official title
No, it is a resource, not a flaw
items.explanation: Power is a neutral resource. What matters is how honestly it is used.

items.prompt: Two ideas are equally good. One gets used and one is shelved. Which explanation fits this unit's model best?
choices: The shelved idea was probably technically weaker too
The used idea came from the more popular student
The used idea reached someone able to act on it
The shelved idea broke an unwritten social rule
items.explanation: If quality is equal, the remaining variable is whether the idea reached someone with the capacity to act. The other options guess at hidden weaknesses the model does not need.
items.reference:
Who could actually say yes?
🧑‍🏫 Teacher: can approve the idea (power)
📣 Theo: borrowed the teacher's attention
💡 Priya: right, but never reached the decision
Why: power is the ability to get something adopted, and it belongs to whoever can act, not to the loudest or the most correct.
items.learnMore:
Power is the ability to get things adopted

It is situational: the teacher holds it over the poster, someone else over the lunch menu. Rank, popularity and volume can help, but none of them is the definition.

Common mistake

Equating power with rank or with talking the most.
items.reflection: Think of a group you were in where a good idea went unused. Who could actually have said yes, and did the idea ever reach them?

items.prompt: A person with a high title proposes a change and nobody acts on it. What does this show about the definition of power?
choices: Titles never carry any real power at all
A title is one source, not the same as power
The proposal must have had a hidden flaw in it
Power only exists inside informal friend groups
items.explanation: Power is the ability to get things done. A title is one source of it, so having the title does not guarantee the ability in every case.

It gave Theo the power to approve ideas himself
It proved to everyone the idea was really his
It made the idea better than it was before
items.explanation: Volume got attention from the teacher, who held the power. It did not create power and it did not change the idea.

choices: Whether people praise your ideas in meetings
Whether your title sounds impressive to others
Whether your colleagues agree with you in debate
Whether you can get resources assigned for it
items.explanation: Power is shown by outcomes: adoption, funding and staffing. Praise, titles and agreement can all exist without any of those.

items.prompt: In this unit, what does politics mean in the neutral sense?
choices: Winning every argument by any method available
Getting people with different interests to agree
Running a campaign for an elected public office
items.explanation: It is the coordination mechanism present in every group, not a synonym for scheming.

items.prompt: Which of these is an abuse rather than a neutral skill?
choices: Asking what the decision-maker actually needs
Telling the teacher honestly whose idea it was
Taking credit for someone else's idea
items.explanation: Stealing credit is dishonest. The other two are honest ways of connecting an idea to a decider.

items.prompt: Which of these is a neutral skill?
choices: Finding out what the decider is trying to solve
Spreading rumours about a rival's idea
Exaggerating what an idea is able to deliver
items.explanation: Learning what matters to the decider is coordination. Rumours and exaggeration are abuses.

items.prompt: If you refuse to engage with politics on principle, decisions get...
choices: Decided purely on the merit of each idea
Made by the people who did engage
Postponed until all agree
items.explanation: The alignment problem does not go away, it just goes to others.

items.prompt: Is politics optional in a group whose members want different things?
choices: Yes, as long as everyone involved is honest
Yes, but only in groups that are small
No, the alignment problem exists regardless
items.explanation: Different interests have to be reconciled in any group. Honesty changes how, not whether.

items.prompt: What is the stated goal of studying power in this unit?
choices: Making power visible so it can be reasoned about
Teaching people how to manipulate colleagues
Learning how to avoid every kind of disagreement
items.explanation: The aim is description and deliberate reasoning, not manipulation.

items.prompt: Why does the word politics have a bad reputation?
choices: The neutral skill is against the rules
Its abuses are its most visible examples
Only dishonest people have ever taken part in it
items.explanation: People notice credit-stealing and rumours, and then judge the whole mechanism by them.

items.prompt: Priya honestly tells the teacher the idea was hers. What is that?
choices: An abuse, because it embarrasses Theo in public
An abuse: she wants attention
A neutral skill: it is true and fair
items.explanation: Stating a true fact about authorship is honest coordination, even if it inconveniences someone.

items.prompt: A teammate says: I do not do politics, the best idea just wins. What is the most accurate reply?
choices: That is right, since merit settles every case
Alignment still happens, just led by whoever engages
That works only if the group is quite small
That holds as long as the idea is technically sound
items.explanation: Different interests still need reconciling. Opting out only changes who does the reconciling.
items.reference:
Neutral skill versus abuse
✅ Telling the teacher honestly whose idea it was
❌ Taking credit for someone else's idea
✅ Learning what the decider is trying to solve
❌ Inventing a problem to look vital
Why: politics in the neutral sense is aligning people with different interests; honesty is what separates it from abuse.
items.learnMore:
Politics is coordination, with honesty as the boundary

Every group with different interests has to reconcile them somehow. Refusing to think about it leaves the outcome to people who did.

Common mistake

Treating all of politics as dirty, which hands influence to those who do not share the squeamishness.
items.reflection: Pick a decision you saw made at school or work. Which interests had to line up for it to happen, and was anything done dishonestly along the way?

items.prompt: Which action crosses from neutral coordination into abuse?
choices: Claiming a benefit the proposal does not deliver
Asking a trusted colleague to back the idea
Learning which metric the decider is judged on
Mentioning honestly who did most of the work
items.explanation: The test is honesty. Claiming an effect the proposal lacks is deception, while the other three are open and true.

It claims anyone with power is always dishonest
It avoids saying how decisions are really made

choices: Professional norms are rarely written down anywhere
Alignment matters only when someone is dishonest
Different interests must still be reconciled into one decision
Rules bind only the least powerful people
items.explanation: Professionalism sets manners, but it does not make people's interests the same. The reconciliation still has to happen.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT one of the four sources of power?
choices: Volume in meetings
Expertise
Relationships with colleagues
items.explanation: The four are formal authority, expertise, relationships and information. Volume is not among them.

items.prompt: Formal authority lets someone...
choices: Be trusted without having any record
Directly allocate budget or priorities
Know what the leaders care about most
items.explanation: Formal authority is the power that comes with a role to assign resources.

items.prompt: Expertise as a source of power is built by...
choices: Being promoted quickly by a manager
Becoming friends with the leadership team
Being right on the record, repeatedly
items.explanation: People stop double-checking you after you have been right many times.

items.prompt: Relationships as a source mean people back you because...
choices: They trust you, not only the pitch
You outrank every one of them
You know a secret about each of them
items.explanation: Trust built through reliable follow-through is what makes backing possible.

items.prompt: Information as a source means...
choices: Keeping facts hidden from other people
Knowing what decision-makers already care about
Owning the largest spreadsheet in the department
items.explanation: It is about context: what has been tried and what leaders are trying to improve.

items.prompt: Which source can arrive overnight?
choices: Expertise, once it is earned
Relationships earned through years of follow-through
Formal authority, through a promotion
items.explanation: A new role can be granted in one conversation. The others take repeated real interactions.

items.prompt: Which source is the slowest to build?
choices: Expertise
Authority
Contacts
items.explanation: It needs a visible record of being right enough times that people stop checking.

items.prompt: Do the four sources require dishonesty to acquire?
choices: Yes, at least two of the four sources do
No, they are what a good colleague builds
Yes, but only in very large companies
items.explanation: Track record, trust, context and role are all ordinary and honest to build.

items.prompt: A new hire with no record has a proposal vouched for by a colleague who trusts them. Which source is doing the work?
choices: Expertise, because the colleague knows the topic well
Relationships, through trust lent by the colleague
Formal authority, because a director makes the call
Information, because the proposal is still quite new
items.explanation: The colleague is spending their own credibility. Expertise cannot be borrowed on day one because the new hire has no record.
items.reference:
Four sources of power
🏛️ Formal authority: allocate directly
🧠 Expertise: judgment accepted without re-checking
🤝 Relationships: people back you because they trust you
🗺️ Information: know what deciders care about
Why: three of the four are patient investments; only formal authority can arrive in a single conversation.
items.learnMore:
Each source is built differently

Authority is granted, information is gathered, relationships are earned through follow-through, and expertise is earned by being right on the record.

Common mistake

Assuming expertise alone will carry a proposal in a place where you have no record yet.
items.reflection: Which of the four sources do you hold most of in your current group, and which one would you start building first?

items.prompt: A manager's technical calls have been right so often that people stop double-checking them. Why is this source hard to speed up?
choices: It needs a public record built over many cases
It depends entirely on a person's job title
It can only be handed out by top leaders
It disappears whenever the team becomes larger
items.explanation: Expertise is accumulated evidence of being right. It cannot be granted, only earned over time.

items.explanation: Knowing the decider's metric is information. Using it does not require rank, a record or friendship.

Authority, information, relationships, then expertise
Relationships, authority, information, then expertise
items.explanation: Authority can be granted at once, information takes weeks of attention, relationships take months of follow-through, and expertise takes the longest.

items.prompt: What does a sponsor do for a proposal?
choices: Writes the whole technical design
Proofreads the finished document
Spends power or credibility on it
items.explanation: A sponsor is someone with enough power to back the proposal with their own capacity.

items.prompt: What does gate 1 ask?
choices: Does it reach someone who can act on it?
Is the proposal cheap enough to afford?
Is the proposal formatted in the usual way?
items.explanation: Gate 1 is about reaching a person with relevant power.

items.prompt: What does gate 2 ask?
choices: Is the design technically correct throughout?
Is it framed around the sponsor's accountability?
Is the proposal short enough to read quickly?
items.explanation: Gate 2 is about connecting the proposal to what the sponsor is responsible for.

items.prompt: What does framing mean here?
choices: Making the document look much nicer
Adding even more technical evidence to it
Explaining the proposal in the sponsor's terms
items.explanation: Framing shows how the proposal helps with something the sponsor already owns.

items.prompt: A correct proposal with no sponsor usually ends up...
choices: Shelved, correct but unadopted
Funded by default
Rejected outright as being wrong
items.explanation: With nobody to act on it, nothing happens, and that is different from being rejected.

items.prompt: Good idea, not this quarter, from a budget holder suggests...
choices: A gate 1: no sponsor
A gate 2 failure: framing
A gate 0 failure: the design is bad
items.explanation: The sponsor exists and agrees, but the proposal does not touch what they are measured on.

items.prompt: Likes in a general channel but no follow-up suggests...
choices: A gate 2 failure: the framing was wrong
A hidden design flaw
A gate 1 failure: no sponsor reached
items.explanation: Visibility is not the same as reaching someone who can act.

items.prompt: Is technical correctness enough for adoption?
choices: No, it is necessary but not sufficient
Yes, as long as the proposal is clearly written
Yes, once it is posted
items.explanation: Correctness gets a proposal to the gate. It does not carry it through.

items.prompt: A budget holder agrees the risk is real but defers the work. What is the most useful next step?
choices: Find a different sponsor straight away
Rewrite the design with much more technical depth
Reframe the same pitch around a metric they own
Resubmit unchanged next quarter and simply wait
items.explanation: The sponsor exists, so the failure is framing. Walking away wastes the relationship and more depth does not address their metric.
items.reference:
Three gates
0️⃣ Is the proposal technically sound?
1️⃣ Does it reach someone who can act on it?
2️⃣ Is it framed around that person's accountability?
Why: a proposal has to clear every gate; failing gate 1 and gate 2 both look like shelved from outside.
items.learnMore:
Sponsor and framing are separate gates

A sponsor is someone with the power to spend capacity or credibility on your proposal. Framing makes the proposal speak to what that person is accountable for.

Common mistake

Treating every shelved proposal as the same failure.
items.reflection: Think of a request you made that went nowhere. Did it fail to reach someone who could act, or did it reach them without speaking to what they care about?

items.prompt: A proposal is posted in a broad channel and only gets compliments. Which diagnosis fits best?
choices: The framing was wrong for the sponsor involved
No sponsor was reached; find who owns the problem
The technical design must contain a hidden flaw
The organization does not value this kind of work
items.explanation: Nobody with power over the problem engaged, which is a gate 1 failure. Nothing here shows a design flaw or a values problem.

choices: Prove it is cheaper than the other alternatives
Show that the sponsor has the longest tenure
Persuade them to approve funding all by themselves
Make vouching worth spending their own trust
items.explanation: Such a sponsor lends credibility rather than money, so the proposal must be worth that spend to them.

items.prompt: What stayed identical across all three attempts?
choices: The sponsor who was approached
The framing used
The technical proposal
items.explanation: Only the path and the pitch changed. The design was the same each time.

items.prompt: Why did Attempt 1 fail?
choices: No sponsor was reached
The design had a flaw
The manager disagreed with the approach
items.explanation: It was posted to a general channel and nobody with power over the problem took it on.

items.prompt: What was the infrastructure manager measured on in Attempt 2?
choices: Improving the sustainability of on-call
Reducing infrastructure cost
Shipping more features
items.explanation: The proposal did not touch cost, so it was not prioritized.

items.prompt: What did Attempt 3 emphasize?
choices: Savings on infrastructure spending
The overall quality of the written documentation
A bottleneck on the few engineers who handle rollbacks
items.explanation: It was a true effect of the same proposal that matched a metric the manager's boss tracked.

items.prompt: How many of the three requirements did Attempt 2 meet?
items.explanation: It was correct and had a sponsor, but the framing missed the sponsor's metric.

items.prompt: What did the outcomes of Attempts 1 and 2 look like from outside?
choices: One of them was a clear and open rejection
Both looked like silence
Both were adopted
items.explanation: That is why the outcome alone does not tell you which gate failed.

items.prompt: After Attempt 2, what was the right move?
choices: Drop that sponsor and look for another
Post it in the channel for a second time
Reframe the pitch for the same sponsor
items.explanation: The sponsor relationship was already there. The pitch needed to change, not the person.

items.prompt: What does Attempt 3 show about the organization?
choices: It could act on the idea through the right path
It never valued engineering work at all
It had been deliberately blocking the proposal
items.explanation: The identical idea was adopted once it reached the right person framed the right way.

items.prompt: An engineer's proposal is praised in a channel and then nothing happens. Which gate most likely failed?
choices: Gate 2, because the framing was slightly off
Gate 0, because the design itself was wrong
None, because adoption simply takes some time
Gate 1, because no one able to act took it on
items.explanation: Praise without follow-up is the pattern of visibility without a sponsor.
items.reference:
Same proposal, three attempts
1️⃣ General channel: correct, no sponsor
2️⃣ Infra manager: + sponsor, wrong framing
3️⃣ Same manager: + framing on on-call load → adopted
Why: only the combination of correct, sponsored and framed predicts adoption; the technical content never changed.
items.learnMore:
Read the failure, not just the silence

Attempts 1 and 2 both ended quietly but needed different next moves: find the person, or reframe to the person you have.

Common mistake

Assuming the organization is broken after a single shelved attempt.
items.reflection: For something of yours that has stalled, which of the three columns is actually missing, and what is the cheapest way to check?

items.prompt: After a manager says not this quarter, an engineer concludes the company does not value engineering. What is wrong with that conclusion?
choices: The manager was assumed to have no budget authority
The design was treated as more important than it is
Framing may have missed the manager's metric
Managers were assumed never to change their minds
items.explanation: One deferral does not show the organization is dysfunctional. Check whether the pitch connected to what the sponsor is measured on.

About 80%
items.explanation: 0.70 times 0.90 is 0.63. Alignment alone (90%) or capacity alone (70%) ignores that both must be present. These are teaching numbers, not measured data.

items.prompt: An honest reframe means...
choices: Changing the design to suit the sponsor
Saying whatever the sponsor wants to hear
Emphasizing a true effect it already has
items.explanation: The effect was real before anyone named it.

items.prompt: A hollow reframe is one that...
choices: Invents or inflates a connection
Names a real benefit of the proposal first
Is shorter than the pitch
items.explanation: Hollow means the claimed link does not actually follow from what the proposal does.

items.prompt: What is a good test of honest framing?
choices: Does the sponsor feel flattered by the pitch?
Would the claim survive the sponsor checking it?
Is the pitch short enough to fit one page?
items.explanation: Honest claims hold when checked against reality.

items.prompt: What is the cost of a hollow framing that gets found out?
choices: It makes the proposal noticeably cheaper
It makes the sponsor patient
It spends trust that is slow to rebuild
items.explanation: The damage extends to every future request.

items.prompt: Attempt 3's on-call point was...
choices: Already a true effect of the proposal
Invented specially for the pitch
Unrelated to the rollback work
items.explanation: Automating rollback really did reduce the dependence on a few engineers.

items.prompt: When a sponsor backs a proposal, they are lending...
choices: Their title
Some of their own credibility
Their whole calendar for a full year
items.explanation: Their reputation is partly at stake if the proposal fails.

items.prompt: What happens if you return to a sponsor only with new asks?
choices: The sponsor trusts you more each time
The asks get easier
The relationship wears down
items.explanation: A relationship needs something flowing back, like reliability and help with their priorities.

items.prompt: Rollback will eliminate all future outages. What is that?
choices: An overclaim
An honest reframe of the pitch
A harmless technical detail to include
items.explanation: Rollback shortens recovery from one kind of failure. It does not prevent outages in general.

items.prompt: Which of these is an honest reframe of automated rollback for a manager measured on on-call load?
choices: It will remove the need for any on-call rotation
It guarantees outages will no longer ever happen
It will cut infrastructure spending in half
It removes the dependence on a few engineers for rollbacks
items.explanation: Only the first is a real consequence of the proposal. The others claim effects automated rollback does not produce.
items.reference:
Honest versus hollow
✅ A true effect, emphasized
❌ An invented or inflated effect
✅ Survives the sponsor checking it
❌ Collapses when checked
Why: framing chooses which true effect to name first; it does not create effects the proposal lacks.
items.learnMore:
The test is whether it survives scrutiny

If the sponsor asked to see the reasoning, an honest reframe would hold. A hollow one spends trust that takes a long time to rebuild.

Common mistake

Treating any emphasis as dishonest, or any claim as fine if it persuades.
items.reflection: Recall a time someone pitched you using your own priorities. Was it honest, and how could you tell?

items.prompt: A proposal truly has no effect on anything the possible sponsors are measured on. What is the honest path?

Drop the technical content and pitch only benefits
Say so, and look for a sponsor whose goals it serves
Wait for the company to value engineering more
items.explanation: Framing cannot add effects. If none matches, the honest options are to find a different sponsor or wait for incentives to change.
